PHSCS 587

Subthreshold swing

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how gate coupling changes the logarithmic slope of weak-inversion current

Weak inversion contains mobile carriers even below threshold. In a long-channel thermionic model, diffusion dominates and ID is proportional to exp[(VGS − Vth)/(mUT)] × [1 − exp(−VDS/UT)], where UT = kT/q is thermal voltage.

Subthreshold swing S = dVGS/dlog₁₀ID = ln(10)mUT is measured in volts per current decade. Smaller S means fewer gate volts are needed for a tenfold current change. At 300 K, the positive-capacitance thermionic ideal m = 1 gives about 59.5 mV/decade.

Depletion coupling makes m greater than one. Short-channel electrostatics, traps and nonideal transport can further alter the measured swing. The familiar room-temperature limit belongs to this stated mechanism and is not a universal bound on every proposed switch.

Example

At 300 K with m = 1.5, S ≈ 89.3 mV/decade. Reducing gate voltage by 0.179 V therefore reduces the modeled current by about two decades, or a factor of 100, at fixed drain bias.

Practice

1. Why does a larger m make an off-state current harder to suppress using the gate?

Compare gate voltage with the induced surface-potential change.

A larger m means poorer gate control of the surface potential, so a larger gate-voltage change is required for the same exponential change in carrier population and current.
